paras: The shooting of Victor Davidson was a street shooting in Charlotte, North Carolina, on the night of Monday, June 20, 1881, in which one of three young white men fired at two Black men and wounded Davidson in the forehead. Davidson's condition was not known when the story appeared, and it was reported in his home town of Yorkville, South Carolina, because he had lived there.

Davidson, called "Vick" in the Charlotte account, was a waiter at Shannonhouse's boarding house in Charlotte and had come from Yorkville. Between ten and eleven o'clock that Monday night he and another Black man, Wm. Wheeler, took a walk toward the old Richmond & Danville depot.

Near the railroad crossing the two men passed three young white men, one of whom caught Davidson by the coat, "evidently thinking him some one else," according to the Charlotte Observer. Words were exchanged, and Davidson and Wheeler walked on. On their way back the groups met again at about the same place and exchanged words a second time. After the Black men had gone a short distance, someone in "the white crowd" fired three pistol shots at them, and one struck Davidson in the forehead, "just above, or nearly between, the eyes."
A letter from Charlotte described the shooters as "some parties unknown" and the wound as severe. No arrest, inquest or later report on Davidson's condition appears in the coverage.

The only report found ran in the Yorkville Enquirer of June 30, 1881, under the headline "Shot in the Head." The Enquirer combined a private letter from Charlotte with the Charlotte Observer's account, which it said agreed with the letter, and presented the story as news of "a Yorkville colored man." Neither the letter nor the Observer, as quoted, named the shooters or commented on them, and the Observer's version suggested the first encounter was a case of mistaken identity.
